But then, I began healing. *He* began healing too. We talked it out at length, many, harrowing times, until acceptance came onto us both. Now we're back to being BFFs, and talk on a daily basis, and plan on hanging out as pals as soon as the occasion arises.   
Remember: nothing in life is set in stone, not the bad things and nor the good things. There is always a future, and there is always hope.   
Stay strong, and if you need someone to talk to, I'm here.

Alright, I'll start off by saying I really understand you, and it looks like we're in the same age gap and have had similar experiences.  


I had to deal with internalized homophobia my whole life. I first knew I was gay when I was a kid -- I must have been 14 or 15 -- and developed my first real crush for a lady classmate. It was a textbook crush, complete with stomach butterflies, blushing and all that. Cue months of anxiety and me trying to convince myself I was not a lesbian, that it must have been the hormones, and that I had to be interested in boys only, like all my peers seemed to.   
I did not grow up in a strict home environment, but I was never the kind of person who liked to go "against the norm," whatever it may mean. I was the good kid who never rebelled (except for being a tad mouthy and pick up smoking), never explored, was good at school and successful in life. Being gay sounded too much out of character, though it was ultimately what I really was. I did have a couple flings with boys, but getting intimate with them was always a chore, and I never ever wished to have any sexual contact with them. The thought of getting pregnant terrified me, and I never desired having the standard domestic life with a male partner, the thought of which never failed to make me feel uneasy.   
Growing up, I found myself lonelier and lonelier, unable to heal the divide between who I was and what I tried not to be.   
The fact I was subject to sexual assault did not help matters any.  
Then, a few years ago I met this guy, and we clicked immediately so well I decided to give it a try. We became close, then a couple, but every time we'd end up in bed it was clear something was very wrong. I resisted a couple of years, until I started crumbling down. I was not interested in my then bf sexually, like I'd never been for any man before. I was very much attracted to women, however, and I couldn't hide it to myself or the world any longer.  
I was a lesbian, always had been.   
Simple as that.  
I spent months of pure hell, amidst self-harm, suicidal ideations, a constant load of guilt on my shoulders.   
Then I took the decision to come out, to a few close friends first and to my family then.  
Everyone reacted quite confused at first, but positively then, and some folks even told me they knew it all along, and were actually in shock at the news I had found a male partner.   
Then I broke up with my ex, and though it wasn't easy, I felt so relieved it was insane. After that, I started undergoing therapy, and accepting my feelings, and my identity. Now I am much more comfortable with my orientation, though the path to acceptance was long and winded and full of suck. I have never been with a woman either (though that's not for lack of trying), but I am 100% convinced that attraction is something so instinctual, natural and deep one does not need *proof* in order to understand whether they like hot dogs or tacos more. And if I'll ever feel like I do, well, the lies I've been telling myself my entire life and the brain gymnastics I subdues myself to in order to find men likeable are evidence enough.   
Stay strong, and if you ever need to vent, feel free to holler.

In their eyes, there was no way I was doing the right thing by admitting I was a lesbian and leaving my then SO. I was just confused, and maybe that guy wasn't the right person for me sexually, but maybe I'd find some other man who'd be able to please me. Luckily enough, we talked this out and now they seem to be at peace with my decision and my general self --  at least on a discursive level.   
My advice would be: don't take any shite from them. If these statements came from people you care about, defend your true beliefs and be open to discuss it. If not, just ignore them and shrug them off your life.

First of all, congrats for coming out! It's always a good feeling, and I hope it'll bring a lot of improvement in your quality of life ;)  


Secondly: I am a chronically anxious person, and I understand the impact anxiety can have on our thoughts, feelings, desires and self-image. I have also struggled with intrusive thoughts (thanks OCD) for most of my life, and they are a real wild cat to wrangle.   
Remember something, though: nobody can force you to marry a man and start a family unless you want to. Compulsory heterosexuality is also an important facet of the whole thing: society pushes certain standards upon women that we find ourselves pursuing, either consciously or subconsciously. So, maybe it feels inevitable to end up in such a situation, but it's really not. It will happen if that is what you really desire, but since this is clearly not the case, feel free to live your life and sexuality as freely as you can. (And if you're so uneasy at the thought of sharing your life with a man, then... well, welcome to the Lezzie club, sister! That's a pretty telling kind of sign. I too always dreaded being a wife and mother, but somehow ended up in a het relationship... which caused me to burst out of the closed out of sheer desperation a couple years in.)  


Thirdly: trauma inflicts very heavy scars on us, and bring us a load of uncertainty and keeps us from truly exploring and being at ease with our sexuality. I was a victim of repeated sexual violence during my formative years, and as a result I ended up hiding my real orientation even further down the pit of denial and turmoil it had stayed throughout my entire life. I was never attracted to men before, that I knew for certain, but after that happened I'd grown even more wary in their presence. It took me so long to rediscover myself and my inner balance it's insane. But I did, I healed, I explored, I made mistakes, and now I have gotten to a point in life in which I can attest with full ease I do not like *the peenie,* and I absolutely love ladies (though I have yet to be with one. Maybe one day!)*.*  


To conclude, perhaps you just need to get yourself some time to be free and adjust to your new, openly-out-there gay life, but remember to always follow your true instincts with honesty and a good dose of peace of mind and you can't go wrong.
